The later codicils merely adjusted the quantum and mechanics of Kevin Fletcher’s lifetime benefits; they did not revoke and re‑execute the will, replace the charitable remainderman, or alter the basic split‑interest structure. Second, even assuming the original life interest was drafted too broadly—because of possible residence improvements and other expenses—§ 2055(e)(3) expressly authorizes post‑mortem judicial reformation to “qualify” a split‑interest transfer for the charitable deduction, with the reformation relating back to the date of death. Section 2055(e)(3) allows reformation only where the original instrument was susceptible of being conformed to the statutory forms. Here, the reformation fundamentally changed Fletcher’s interest from an indeterminate, consumption-based life estate into a fixed annuity. Allowing taxpayers to rely on an earlier will date despite substantive codicils would undermine that temporal line and invite manipulation.

Section 1382(c) creates a tightly integrated scheme that the Secretary’s policy disrupts.

First, § 1382(c)(2)(A) mandates *retrospective* monthly accounting: the benefit for month N is based on income in month N–2. Congress then carved out a narrow exception in § 1382(c)(5) for the initial eligibility period, allowing the Secretary to base benefits for the first (and at most the second) month on “the income of such individual *in such month* and other relevant circumstances in such month.”

Two features of this language are crucial.

1. **Temporal limitation.** For the first (and optionally second) month, Congress expressly directed the agency to look to “such month,” not to re‑use the same income item in later calculations. By month three the statute compels a return to the two‑month look‑back. Under that mandatory structure, the only income that may affect month three is income actually received in month one—not income that has already been fully accounted for as “actual” income in the first‑month calculation.

2. **“Relevant circumstances” and nonrecurring income.** Congress required that the initial-month calculation consider “other relevant circumstances in such month.” The fact that a payment is a one‑time “gate release” benefit, tied to discharge and not to ongoing support, is precisely such a circumstance. Treating that nonrecurring sum as if it were continuing income—so that it depresses benefits for multiple months—ignores its one‑time character and violates the command to account for “relevant circumstances” *in that month*.

The agency’s “transitional computation cycle” effectively converts a single month’s income into three months’ income, creating a triple deduction nowhere authorized in the text. It nullifies Congress’s carefully limited initial‑month exception and undermines the statute’s remedial purpose of providing subsistence‑level support when eligibility is regained. Under the statutory language and structure, the one‑time payment can be counted once, not repeatedly; the Carter Class must prevail.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) establishes a clear default rule: in an RMA system, a month’s benefit is based on income from two months earlier. Congress then created a narrow, explicit departure from that rule in § 1382(c)(2)(A)(i)–(iii) and § 1382(c)(5): for the first (and, at the Secretary’s option, the second) month of eligibility, benefits must be computed on the *actual income and circumstances* in that month, not via the two‑month look‑back.

That framework makes sense only if all income actually received in the “first (and possibly second)” month is accounted for *once*—in the transitional months for which Congress authorized individualized, real‑time calculations. A one‑time “gate release” payment is the quintessential “relevant circumstance” that Congress required the Secretary to consider in that initial computation and then leave behind when the system reverts to the mechanical RMA formula.

The Secretary’s policy contravenes that structure. By treating the same nonrecurring payment (and in‑kind support) as (1) income in the first transitional month and then (2) again as prior‑month income in subsequent months, the agency effectively triple‑counts a single, discrete event. Nothing in the statutory text authorizes repeated imputation of the same income; the statute speaks of “income of such individual during such month,” not “income events that may be leveraged across multiple months at the agency’s discretion.”

Moreover, § 1382(c)(5) directs the Secretary, in setting RMA rules, to “take into account the relevant circumstances” of recipients. A system that ignores the nonrecurring nature of gate‑release payments—and treats them as if they were continuing income—fails that command and undermines Congress’s evident goal: to smooth administration without distorting benefits for those re‑entering eligibility.

Because the Secretary’s guidance conflicts with the statutory design, it is unlawful, and the Carter Class must prevail.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) establishes RMA as the default rule—benefits in month N are based on income from month N–2. But Congress simultaneously carved out a targeted exception for the first (and at the Secretary’s option, second) month of eligibility, directing that benefits then be determined by “the income and other relevant circumstances in such month.” 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(2)(A), (5).

That text does two things. First, it displaces the two‑month look‑back for the initial month(s) and mandates a month‑specific, real‑time calculation. Second, by requiring consideration of “relevant circumstances in such month,” Congress instructs that the temporal character of income—recurring vs. nonrecurring—is itself a relevant circumstance. A one‑time gate release payment tied to leaving detention is, by definition, not part of the recipient’s ongoing income stream in later months.

The Secretary’s guidance nullifies that structure. By applying the transitional rules prospectively in month one, then re‑importing the same one‑time payment through RMA in months two and three, the agency effectively treats a single, nonrecurring sum as if it were received three times. That “triple deduction” is not retrospective accounting; it is double‑counting plus one. Nothing in §§ 1382(c)(2)(A) or (5) authorizes the same payment to reduce benefits beyond the month in which it is “income … in such month.”

At minimum, the statute is ambiguous as to whether nonrecurring, release‑related payments may be spread over multiple months. In a remedial program designed to provide subsistence‑level support, such ambiguity must be resolved in favor of beneficiaries, and against an interpretation that mechanically compounds reductions untethered to actual, ongoing income.

Because the Secretary’s policy disregards the mandated focus on month‑specific “relevant circumstances” and impermissibly multiplies the impact of a one‑time payment, it is contrary to the statute and the Carter Class must prevail.

Under 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(2)(A), Congress adopted Retrospective Monthly Accounting as the default but carved out a clear, targeted exception: for “the first month for which an individual is eligible” (and, at the Secretary’s option, the second), benefits must be computed based on “the income and other circumstances in such month.” Section 1382(c)(5) reinforces that this transitional period exists to accommodate “relevant circumstances” at the onset of eligibility.

For Carter Class members, the “gate release” payment is paradigmatic nonrecurring income—a single, one-time event tied to release from detention. In month one, that payment is a “relevant circumstance” and may properly reduce benefits. But nothing in § 1382(c)(2)(A) or § 1382(c)(5) authorizes treating that same nonrecurring event as if it were ongoing income for later months.

The Secretary’s guidance unlawfully collapses the statutory distinction between (1) actual income in the initial month(s) and (2) past income in the RMA look‑back period. By allowing a one‑time payment to be charged prospectively in month one and again retroactively in months two and three, the agency effectively counts the same income three times. That is incompatible with a scheme that keys each month’s benefit to “income” for a defined period, not to isolated windfalls replayed indefinitely.

Moreover, Congress’s express concern with “relevant circumstances” in the initial period necessarily includes the nonrecurring character of such payments. Treating a gate‑release payment as if it were recurring defeats that command and undermines the statute’s remedial purpose of providing subsistence‑level support upon reentry.

At minimum, the text is ambiguous, and under ordinary canons governing welfare legislation, ambiguities must be resolved in favor of beneficiaries. The agency’s triple‑deduction rule is neither compelled by the statute nor reasonable. Carter Class should prevail.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) establishes RMA as a *monthly* accounting system keyed to “income . . . in the second month preceding the month for which such income is considered.” Section 1382(c)(5) then creates a narrow transitional exception for the *first* (and optionally second) month of eligibility, requiring that benefits be computed based on “the income of such individual *and other relevant circumstances in such month*.”  

Read together, these provisions do two things: (1) tie benefit calculations to specific months, with each month’s benefit reflecting income assigned to that month, and (2) in the transitional period, require a fresh, month-specific assessment that expressly takes account of “relevant circumstances.” A nonrecurring gate-release payment, tied to the single event of release from custody, is quintessentially a “relevant circumstance” of that first month only. Nothing in the statute authorizes the Secretary to fraction that one-time payment across multiple subsequent months or to let it echo through later RMA computations once its actual receipt month has already been used in setting benefits.  

The Secretary’s guidance effectively converts a one-time transitional income event into a multi-month offset. In month one, the payment is counted prospectively under § 1382(c)(5); in later months it reappears through the two‑month look‑back, producing a triple deduction. That double‑counting contradicts the statute’s temporal pairing of income with specific months and nullifies the command to consider “relevant circumstances” in the transitional months—i.e., that this was nonrecurring, not ongoing income.  

At minimum, any ambiguity must be resolved in favor of beneficiaries in this remedial program. The Carter Class’s reading honors the text, structure, and purpose of RMA; the Secretary’s reading creates an unjustified windfall to the government by charging the same dollar of income against benefits multiple times. The statute does not permit that outcome.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) mandates Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA): after any applicable transition, “the amount of the benefit for a month shall be determined on the basis of income … in the second month preceding such month.” Section 1382(c)(5) then authorizes a “transitional computation period” when an individual becomes (or regains) eligibility, allowing the Secretary to base “the amount of the benefit for such first month (and, at the option of the Secretary, the second month)” on “the income… and other relevant circumstances in such month.”

Nothing in either provision limits income to being counted only once, or exempts nonrecurring income from the subsequent, statutorily required RMA look‑back. To the contrary, Congress’s express design is: (1) a short, discretionary transition period; then (2) a rigid two‑month look‑back for all income, however characterized. The Carter Class’s “one‑time means one‑month” theory would have to be written into the statute; it is not there.

The Secretary’s policy is precisely what § 1382(c)(5) authorizes: for individuals regaining eligibility, a two‑month transitional computation to reflect “actual” circumstances, followed by reversion to normal RMA in month three. Under that reversion, the month‑one gate‑release payment—indisputably “income” when received—must, by the statute’s own terms, be part of the income “in the second month preceding” month three. Treating that income as relevant in month one and again as part of the historical income base for month three is not “triple deduction”; it is the predictable consequence of the very retrospective structure Congress chose.

Nor does “other relevant circumstances” in § 1382(c)(5) tacitly authorize the Secretary to excise nonrecurring income from future RMA months. That clause concerns what may be considered in the transition months, not an atextual exception to the core RMA mandate. At minimum, the statute is ambiguous on this point, and the Secretary’s long‑standing, reasoned interpretation warrants deference. The regulations thus lawfully permit the challenged offsets, and judgment should be entered for the Secretary.

The Secretary should prevail because his treatment of the one‑time gate payment is fully consistent with the text, structure, and purpose of 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(2)(A) and § 1382(c)(5).

First, Congress expressly adopted Retrospective Monthly Accounting: benefits in a given month are computed “on the basis of income… in the second month preceding such month.” § 1382(c)(2)(A). Nothing in the statute excludes nonrecurring payments from that income base or limits their effect to a single month. To the contrary, Congress understood that any income in the budget month—recurring or not—would affect benefits in a later month. The Carter Class’s “count-once” rule appears nowhere in the text.

Second, § 1382(c)(5) authorizes a special “first month” (and optional second month) computation to reflect actual circumstances at the start of eligibility. The Secretary used that authority via the “transitional computation cycle,” which explicitly applies the prospective method for the first two months and then reverts to standard RMA in the third. That the same payment influences several months is not “triple deduction” but the inevitable arithmetic when one month’s income is used both prospectively (for the true first month) and retrospectively (when that same month becomes the budget month two months later), exactly as Congress prescribed.

Third, the agency reasonably concluded that the nonrecurring character of income is not a “relevant circumstance” that overrides RMA’s core design. At a minimum, the statute is ambiguous on this point. The Secretary’s interpretation—embodied in detailed, longstanding guidance—is reasonable and therefore entitled to deference.

Accordingly, the challenged policy faithfully implements the RMA system Congress enacted, and judgment should be entered for the Secretary.

The statutory text, structure, and purpose support the Secretary.

First, 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(2)(A) establishes Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA): benefits for a month are based on income “for the second month preceding.” Nothing in that subsection carves out nonrecurring payments from this formula or limits their effect to one month. Congress adopted a uniform retrospective system knowing that any income in a given month would necessarily affect at least one future month’s benefit.

Second, § 1382(c)(5) creates a narrow exception for the *first* (and, at the Secretary’s option, second) month of eligibility, allowing computation based on “income . . . in such month” and “other relevant circumstances in such month.” This language modifies *which* month’s data may be used for initial eligibility; it does not prohibit that same income from being part of the historical record for later RMA months. Carter’s reading would effectively add words Congress did not use: that nonrecurring income “shall be counted only once.”

Third, the Secretary’s “transitional computation cycle” reasonably harmonizes these provisions. For months one and two, benefits are based on contemporaneous income and circumstances, as § 1382(c)(5) allows. Beginning in month three, the statute’s default RMA rule applies. Treating Carter’s gate release payment as income in month one, which by design then enters the RMA pipeline, is not “triple counting”; it is the mechanical operation of the retrospective formula applied equally to all income.

Finally, nothing in the statute elevates the “nonrecurring” nature of income to a mandatory “relevant circumstance” overriding RMA in later months. Congress left implementation details to the agency, and the Secretary’s system promotes administrative consistency and prevents windfalls, aligning with the overall income‑replacement purpose of the benefit program. The Secretary’s interpretation is faithful, reasonable, and should be upheld.

The statutory text, structure, and purpose support the Secretary’s practice.

First, 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c)(2)(A) mandates Retrospective Monthly Accounting, under which “income… in the second month preceding” is used to compute the benefit. Section 1382(c)(5) then creates a narrow exception for the *first* (and optionally second) month of eligibility, allowing the Secretary to base those months on “the income and other relevant circumstances in such month.” Nothing in either provision restricts how that same income must or must not be treated once the system reverts to ordinary RMA in later months. The prohibition of less favourable treatment “on the ground” of part-time status mirrors the language of EU equality law (e.g. sex, race, fixed-term status), where settled case law holds that the protected characteristic need only be a “material” or “effective” reason, not the exclusive reason. Reading “on the ground of” as “solely because of” would set a higher causation bar for part-time workers than for other discrimination regimes, contrary to the Directive’s purpose of equivalent protection.

2. **Purpose of the Directive**  
Directive 97/81 aims to remove discrimination against part‑time workers and to improve the quality of part‑time work. That purpose would be frustrated if employers could avoid liability simply by pointing to a general revenue objective whenever a measure disproportionately burdens part‑time workers. Almost every discriminatory measure can be rationalised as cost-related: that cannot negate protection.

3. **Application to the circuit fee**  
The flat circuit fee affects part‑time workers more harshly: spread over fewer hours and fewer bookings, it materially reduces their net earnings compared to full‑time comparators. Both parties accept that Reeves’s part‑time status was a factor in how the scheme operated on him. That is sufficient: his status clearly formed part of the causal matrix that produced the disadvantage.

4. **Objective justification burden**  
Once less favourable treatment “on the ground” of part‑time status is established, the burden shifts to Stone Rides to justify the practice as a necessary and proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. A blanket, undifferentiated fee, imposed without adjustment for hours worked or earnings, is neither necessary nor proportionate when less discriminatory alternatives (e.g. per‑booking or percentage fees) are plainly available.

First, EU and UK discrimination law uniformly reject a “sole cause” test. In sex, race, and disability discrimination, “on grounds of” has long been interpreted to mean that the protected ground must materially influence the treatment, not exclude any other motive. The Regulations implement Directive 97/81, whose purpose is to prevent structural disadvantage to part‑time workers. Requiring proof that part‑time status was the exclusive reason would make that protection illusory and defeat the Directive’s effet utile.

Second, the “circuit fee” operates in a way that is inherently less favourable to part‑time workers. A flat access fee consumes a much greater proportion of a part‑timer’s earnings and opportunities than a full‑timer’s, so that the same nominal fee produces substantially different economic treatment. Third, the fact that Stone Rides charges all drivers does not answer the claim. Discrimination law recognises that formally identical rules can be unlawfully discriminatory when they are applied in circumstances that systematically disadvantage a protected group and where the protected status is a real reason why the rule is maintained in that form. Here, the company concedes that part‑time status was “a factor.” That is sufficient: the treatment was “on the ground” of part‑time status within the meaning of the Regulations.

Third, even if a multifactor causation test were accepted, Reeves has not shown that his part-time status was an effective reason for the fee. The unchallenged evidence is that the principal reason was commercial: to raise revenue and align with sector norms in a context where Stone Rides did not collect fares directly. That is a status-neutral, objective justification, applicable in the same way to all drivers and necessary for the sustainable operation of the platform.

Accordingly, Reeves has not shown that any less favourable treatment occurred “on the ground” of part-time status within the meaning of the Regulations, and his claim must fail.

Stone Rides Inc should prevail because Reeves has not demonstrated less favourable treatment “on the ground” of part‑time status within the meaning of the 2000 Regulations, properly interpreted in light of Directive 97/81.

First, there is no differential term or condition between part‑time and full‑time workers. The “circuit fee” was identically imposed on *all* drivers as a flat access charge to the booking platform, irrespective of hours worked, income level, or contractual status. A provision that is facially neutral and applied universally cannot, without more, be characterised as less favourable treatment *because* a worker is part‑time.

Second, the undisputed principal reason for the fee is commercial: to generate platform revenue in line with industry practice, where operators do not collect fares directly. That is a legitimate business aim, unconnected with any intention to disadvantage part‑time workers. The Regulations and Directive require a causal nexus: treatment must be *on the ground* of being part‑time, not merely a background circumstance that makes a neutral rule feel harsher in practice. If it sufficed that part‑timers are disproportionately affected by a universally applied charge, the specific “part‑time workers” regime would be transformed into a general proportionality review of all pricing and fee structures, which the Directive does not mandate.

Third, comparability fails in substance. The appropriate comparator is a full‑time driver paying the same absolute fee for the same access. The fact that a full‑timer can amortise the cost over more hours or trips reflects differences in utilisation of the system, not less favourable contractual treatment by the employer.

Accordingly, Reeves has not shown that part‑time status was the legal ground of the impugned treatment, and Stone Rides’ uniform fee policy falls outside the prohibition in the 2000 Regulations.

Stone Rides Inc should succeed because Mr Reeves has not shown that any less favourable treatment was “on the ground” of his part‑time status, as required by the 2000 Regulations properly interpreted in light of Directive 97/81.

Second, the Directive and Regulations are aimed at preventing workers being treated less favourably *because* they are part‑time – i.e. where part‑time status is the operative reason for the impugned treatment, not merely a background characteristic. Construing “on the ground of” to include any situation where part‑time work is one of several contextual factors would dilute the causation requirement and effectively turn neutral, business‑justified rules with incidental disparate impacts into unlawful discrimination, contrary to the Directive’s focus on unjustified differential treatment.

Third, Stone Rides has given a clear, non‑discriminatory explanation: the fee exists to generate revenue and align with sector norms where intermediaries recover platform costs from all users. That is a legitimate aim, pursued consistently and irrespective of contractual hours. Mr Reeves has not shown that his part‑time status, rather than this commercial rationale, was the decisive ground for the fee.

Accordingly, on a proper construction of the Regulations, requiring the claimant to establish that part‑time status was the ground – not merely a correlated circumstance – Stone Rides Inc should prevail.

The court’s task under the Children Act 1989 is not to conduct an abstract inquiry into historical tragedies, but to determine whether there is a current likelihood of significant harm to Child S and what orders are necessary and proportionate to protect her welfare.

Where the Local Authority already has ample, up‑to‑date evidence of safe care, ordering an onerous historical fact‑finding exercise is neither. The court should decline a further fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death because it is unnecessary, disproportionate, and contrary to Child S’s welfare and Article 8 rights.

First, the Children Act 1989 focuses the court on present and future risk, not abstract historical inquiry. To reopen these events years later would require extensive expert and factual inquiry, with no realistic prospect of producing conclusive findings. Third, proportionality and avoidance of delay are central. A complex fact‑finding would consume months, diverting professional and parental focus from Child S’s day‑to‑day needs and prolonging uncertainty, contrary to the statutory requirement to avoid delay in decisions about children. It would effectively punish Ms. Samuels for her traumatic past without clear benefit to Child S.

The court’s paramount duty under the Children Act 1989 is to secure Child S’s safety, not to minimise procedural burden. Where a previous child in the same mother’s care has died in unexplained circumstances, with injuries consistent with non‑accidental trauma, the law requires a rigorous evaluation of potential risk, not an assumption that “the past is different.”

Section 31 CA 1989 permits intervention based not only on actual harm but on a likelihood of significant harm, to be assessed on proven facts (Re H; Re S-B). Here, the only route to understanding whether there is a real, ongoing risk to Child S is to establish, so far as possible, what happened to Child R. The index event is of the gravest kind: an infant death with suggestive injuries, within a context of anger, instability, and substance use. Without knowing whether Child R’s injuries were accidental, neglectful, or inflicted, professionals cannot calibrate what level of vigilance, support, or restriction is required now. In public law proceedings of this seriousness, Article 8 proportionality cuts both ways: any long‑term interference with Ms. Samuels’s and Child S’s family life must be based on clear findings, and conversely, any decision to leave Child S in her sole care must equally rest on a fully informed risk assessment.

A focused, time‑limited fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death is therefore necessary, proportionate, and central to the welfare evaluation of Child S. The court should grant the Local Authority’s application.

The court’s paramount duty under the Children Act 1989 is to protect Child S from a risk of significant harm, not merely to record that she is presently thriving in a highly supported environment. That assessment must be informed by all relevant evidence, including serious, unexplained injuries to a previous child in the same mother’s care.

Child R died with injuries “sometimes associated with shaking or impact trauma.” While there was no criminal conviction, the family court’s task is different: it must evaluate risk on the civil standard, taking into account a wider evidential picture. Unexplained, potentially non‑accidental injuries to a sibling are, by established authority, a classic and weighty indicator of possible future risk. It would be artificial—and dangerous—to disregard that history simply because time has passed or because the criminal process was inconclusive.

The concerns are compounded by Ms. Samuels’s acknowledged vulnerabilities: chronic trauma, impulsivity, cannabis use (including during pregnancy), and a history of anger and conflict in the period around Child R’s death. Without a proper forensic examination of what happened to Child R, the court cannot reliably determine whether those same factors could crystallise into serious harm to Child S if professional oversight is reduced.

A fact‑finding hearing is proportionate to the gravity of the potential harm: the unexplained death of a sibling with suspicious injuries. The temporary diversion of Ms. Samuels’s attention is outweighed by the need to make a fully informed, durable welfare decision about Child S’s long‑term safety. Evaluating only Ms. Samuels’s current presentation, in a supported setting, risks a false sense of security and leaves the court to decide with a critical gap in the evidential record.

Accordingly, to discharge its protective duty, the court should order a fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death.

The court is concerned not merely with how Ms. Samuels is coping today, but with whether there is a real possibility of significant harm to Child S over his whole childhood. Under s.31 Children Act 1989 and the authorities on “likelihood of significant harm” (e.g. Re H, Re S‑B), past serious harm to a sibling, particularly where unexplained and potentially non‑accidental, is a powerful indicator of future risk and must be rigorously examined.

Child R died in Ms. Samuels’s care with injuries consistent with shaking or impact trauma. There is no benign medical explanation. The death occurred in the context of anger, conflict, and substance misuse. Those are precisely the types of stresses that can recur in parenting. Without a careful forensic determination of whether Child R’s death was non‑accidental and, if so, who was responsible or within the “pool of perpetrators,” the court cannot intelligently assess the magnitude of risk to Child S or what level of protective measures are needed.

The fact that Child S is currently thriving in a closely monitored residential assessment does not answer the central question: What happens when that structure and scrutiny fall away, or when Ms. Samuels faces similar emotional or environmental pressures to those existing at the time of Child R’s death? The court cannot safely extrapolate long‑term safety from a short period of supervised care, especially in the shadow of an unexplained fatality.

A fact‑finding hearing is therefore necessary and proportionate. Any additional time or emotional burden for Ms. Samuels is outweighed by the gravity of the issue—a previous child’s unexplained death with suspicious injuries—and the court’s paramount duty to secure Child S’s safety on a sound evidential foundation, not on assumption or hope.

The court’s paramount consideration is Child S’s welfare (Children Act 1989, s.1). To determine whether the s.31 threshold is crossed—“significant harm” or risk thereof—it must assess risk prospectively, drawing on all available evidence, especially serious past unexplained injury to a sibling.

Child R died with injuries “sometimes associated with shaking or impact trauma.” That is not a historic, peripheral concern; it is a potentially non‑accidental death of a baby in Ms. Samuels’s care. The law is clear that past unexplained harm to one child is highly relevant to the risk to another (e.g. Re H (Minors) [1996] AC 563; Re S-B [2009] UKSC 17). The court cannot safely ignore a possible index event of the gravest kind.

Without a fact‑finding hearing, the court is left with a critical evidential gap: was Child R’s death likely non‑accidental, and if so, was Ms. Samuels a possible perpetrator or within a pool of perpetrators? That determination fundamentally shapes the risk assessment. Current positive presentation—while important—cannot by itself neutralise the need to understand whether there is a background of catastrophic, possibly inflicted, injury.

Moreover, Ms. Samuels’s profile—chronic trauma, prior anger and impulsivity, cannabis use in pregnancy—may interact with any unresolved findings about Child R’s death. Professionals’ present observations take place in a highly supported, supervised environment; they do not replicate the stresses of independent parenting over time. The fact‑finding process is designed to give Ms. Samuels a fair opportunity to meet the allegations with disclosure, expert evidence, and representation.

The resources and time required are justified by the magnitude of potential harm—death or serious injury of an infant. To discharge its protective duty lawfully and rationally, the court must base its decision on a full evidential foundation. That requires a fact‑finding hearing into the circumstances of Child R’s death.

The court’s paramount obligation under the Children Act 1989 is to safeguard and promote Child S’s welfare, including protection from the risk of significant harm. That exercise must be grounded in the best available evidence, not assumptions or optimism.

Here, a previous child in Ms. Samuels’s sole care, Child R, died with injuries “sometimes associated with shaking or impact trauma.” Although there was no criminal conviction, the family court’s threshold is the balance of probabilities, and it is precisely in this jurisdiction that unexplained, non-criminally-prosecuted injuries must be evaluated. The gap in understanding how Child R sustained those injuries is not a historical curiosity; it goes directly to whether Child S is at real, ongoing risk of serious physical harm.

The index concerns about Ms. Samuels are not remote or resolved: chronic trauma features in her mental health, a history of anger and impulsivity, and cannabis use including in pregnancy. Those factors overlap with the period surrounding Child R’s unexplained injuries and death. Without a fact‑finding hearing, the court is left to speculate whether those features contributed to non‑accidental harm or were benign. That speculative approach is inconsistent with the protective purpose of s.31.

The fact that Child S is currently thriving within a closely monitored, professionalised environment is reassuring but not determinative. The court must assess risk in the medium and long term, including when supports reduce or end. Only a structured, forensic determination of what more likely than not happened to Child R can inform: (a) whether Ms. Samuels caused or failed to protect from serious harm; (b) whether identified patterns are remediable; and (c) what safeguards are required for Child S.

Accordingly, a fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death is not optional but necessary to discharge the court’s protective duty to Child S.

The Secretary of State should prevail because, on the evidence, Mr. Ho has not discharged the burden of showing a well‑founded fear of persecution for a Refugee Convention reason, nor a real risk of serious harm on return.

First, his core account lacks credibility. The unchallenged country information and official documents confirm that the recognised martyr status of his father exempts him from military service. His entire narrative of being targeted for failing to perform, or buy himself out of, military obligations is therefore inherently implausible. He offers only assertion, unsupported by documentary evidence of any bribe demands or payments, despite claiming a longstanding and systematic extortion.

Second, his explanation for the discrepancies between his claimed assaults and what he told medical staff in River Clinic and Maple District Hospital is unsatisfactory. It is inherently unlikely that a victim of repeated, organised persecution would fabricate ordinary causes of injury to independent medical professionals if he genuinely sought help. The medical records demonstrate only injuries, not their cause, and cannot corroborate his account of persecution.

Third, Mr. Ho never sought protection from the Vietnamese authorities. Under the 2004 Act and established asylum jurisprudence, an applicant must show that state protection is unavailable or ineffective. Here, there is no evidence of any complaint, report, or attempt to escalate matters beyond the allegedly corrupt local actors. Nor has he shown that internal relocation within Vietnam would be unreasonable or unsafe.

Fourth, the timing of his claim—made only once deportation action began after a serious drugs conviction—properly damages his credibility under section 8 of the 2004 Act. His explanations do not overcome the strong inference that the claim is opportunistic.

Taken together, these factors fall far short of establishing a genuine, forward‑looking risk of persecution or serious harm. The refusal of asylum and decision to deport were lawful and proportionate.

The Secretary of State should prevail because Mr. Ho has not discharged the burden of showing a well‑founded fear of persecution under the 1951 Convention, as applied via the 2004 Act.

That directly undermines the central premise that he was at risk of conscription‑related pressure. The River Clinic and Maple District Hospital records prove only that he suffered injuries; they do not corroborate his attribution of those injuries to persecutory attacks. His admitted use of false explanations to medical staff is a significant credibility marker under s.8 of the 2004 Act: if he was willing to mislead treating professionals in Vietnam, the Tribunal can properly be cautious about accepting his unsupported account now.

Third, there is a complete absence of reasonably available supporting evidence: no proof of payments, no police complaints, no attempts to seek protection from higher authorities or party structures. His explanation—that corruption is pervasive—cannot simply displace the expectation, reflected in country guidance, that Vietnam generally operates functioning state protection and internal relocation is often available.

Fourth, the late timing of his asylum claim—only after notice of deportation following a serious drugs conviction—falls squarely within s.8 considerations. This strongly indicates opportunism rather than a genuine, long‑held fear.

Taken together, these factors justify the Secretary of State’s adverse credibility findings and support the conclusion that Mr. Ho has not shown a real risk of Convention persecution or serious harm on return.

The Secretary of State should prevail because Mr. Ho has not discharged even the relatively low burden of proving a well‑founded fear of persecution, and the Secretary of State’s credibility concerns are rational, evidence‑based, and fully aligned with the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004.

His explanation for giving false causes to hospital staff—fear of a corrupt network with reach into local institutions—is plausible and again aligned with known conditions. Third, the late asylum claim and absence of formal complaints in Vietnam fall squarely within s.8 considerations, but they are not determinative. Fear of approaching authorities—whom he reasonably believes to be implicated in the very corruption he fears—is a rational explanation, particularly for someone from an authoritarian context who was later convicted of a drug offence and might reasonably distrust all state actors.

On the country material and the evidence taken as a whole, there is at least a real risk that the same network that previously targeted Mr. Ho would persecute him again, with the added vulnerability of his criminal record and failed deportation. Under the lower standard of proof, he should be granted protection.

Mr. Ho’s claim meets the asylum standard when the correct legal tests are applied to the evidence.

First, the applicable standard is whether there is a “real risk” of serious harm on return, not proof beyond reasonable doubt. Credibility must be assessed in the round. Here, the core of Mr. Ho’s account has been consistent: he was targeted for corrupt payments linked to military service issues; he was assaulted when he could not comply; he fears those same networks will target him again.

Second, his account is independently supported by medical evidence from two different facilities (River Clinic and Maple District Hospital). Both records objectively confirm injuries at the times he claims. His explanation for giving false causes to hospital staff is inherently plausible in a context where the very perpetrators are embedded in local power structures and he feared reprisals for disclosing the truth. Apparent discrepancies in hospital histories therefore enhance, rather than undermine, his fear of local corruption and lack of protection.

Third, the Secretary of State’s reliance on formal exemption due to his father’s martyr status does not answer the point. Mr. Ho’s case is not that he was *lawfully* required to serve, but that corrupt officials wrongly treated him as exploitable. Asylum law protects against persecution by non‑state actors where the state is unwilling or unable to provide effective protection. The absence of formal complaints or receipts for bribes is entirely consistent with fear of those same actors and the futility of challenging entrenched corruption.

Fourth, the late asylum claim is readily explained: he was focused on his criminal proceedings, feared removal, and only then understood the protection route. Delay may affect weight, but cannot be determinative.

Taken together, the medical corroboration, coherent core narrative, and country‑consistent risk of corrupt mistreatment satisfy the 2004 Act’s requirements. Mr. Ho faces a real risk of serious harm on return and should be granted asylum.

Mr. Ho’s claim meets the statutory and international protection thresholds when assessed against the correct legal tests and in light of all the evidence, not isolated credibility challenges.

First, the standard is a “reasonable degree of likelihood” of future persecution, not proof beyond reasonable doubt. The medical reports from two independent facilities in Ho Chi Minh City constitute strong, objective corroboration that Mr. Ho suffered serious physical assaults in Vietnam contemporaneous with his account. The fact that he gave different explanations for his injuries to medical staff is entirely consistent with a person fearing reprisal from powerful local actors—a recognised feature in country guidance on corruption‑driven abuse and non‑state persecution.

Second, the Secretary of State’s reliance on the formal exemption arising from his father’s martyr status is misplaced. Mr. Ho’s case is precisely that, notwithstanding de jure exemption, de facto corruption and entrenched patronage networks exposed him to extortion and violence. That is not rebutted by paperwork attesting to a theoretical exemption; indeed, it is typical in systems where official protections are undermined by local impunity.

Third, the absence of receipts for bribes or formal complaints is unsurprising and should not be held against him. Victims of corrupt officials rarely generate paper trails or complain to the very authorities complicit in their abuse. The 2004 Act requires a holistic assessment of credibility, not an unrealistic expectation of documentary proof of clandestine payments.

Fourth, late assertion of asylum does not, by itself, negate credibility. Mr. Ho offered plausible explanations: fear of authority born of past abuse, lack of legal awareness, and only understanding the protection process when deportation became imminent. Those explanations are consistent with the profile of a vulnerable migrant who has also experienced criminal exploitation in the UK.

Viewed cumulatively, there is at least a real risk that Mr. Ho would again face extortion, violence, and a lack of effective state protection if returned. Under the 2004 Act and the UK’s Refugee Convention and Article 3 ECHR obligations, he should be granted protection.

Steel Horizon should succeed because Jade Energy Ventures (“JEV”) remained the beneficial owner of Iris House until the impugned transfer, making that transfer a transaction at an undervalue within section 423 of the Insolvency Act 1986.

First, any suggestion that Emerald Pension Fund (“EPF”) had a prior beneficial interest under an arrangement governed by foreign law cannot displace the mandatory formalities of English law for English land. Section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925 requires a disposition of an equitable interest to be “in writing signed by the person disposing of the same, or by his agent thereunto lawfully authorised in writing.” Without compliant written evidence of a disposition by JEV, no trust of Iris House in EPF’s favour can be recognised.

Second, the mortgage documents relied on by JEV do not satisfy section 53(1)(b). They are financing instruments, not trust instruments; they record JEV’s position as legal owner and borrower, not as a trustee divesting itself of beneficial title. At best, they are equivocal references to EPF’s economic connection, not a clear, signed declaration by JEV that it is holding Iris House on trust for EPF. Section 53(1)(b) demands certainty as to the existence and terms of any trust; ambiguity is fatal.

Third, the distinction between signatures by the landowner as such and signatures by an agent is critical. The documents are not signed in a capacity that clearly effects a disposition of JEV’s beneficial interest, nor is there evidence of a lawfully authorised agent in writing disposing of that interest. Accordingly, JEV retained the beneficial interest up to the date of transfer.

Given JEV’s retention of beneficial ownership and the timing—shortly after Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce its award—the transfer of Iris House is a classic section 423 transaction at an undervalue intended to put assets beyond creditors’ reach.

Steel Horizon should prevail because Jade Energy Ventures (“JEV”) remained the beneficial owner of Iris House until its post-award transfer, which therefore constituted a transaction at an undervalue under section 423 Insolvency Act 1986.

First, JEV held legal title. To displace the presumption that it also held the beneficial interest, Emerald Pension Fund (“EPF”) must prove a valid trust. JEV relies on (i) an earlier “foreign law” arrangement and (ii) later trust declarations said to be evidenced by mortgage documents.

The foreign-law arrangement is irrelevant unless and until it is shown to create, under English conflict rules, a trust of English land that complies with mandatory English formality requirements. Section 53(1)(b) Law of Property Act 1925 requires any declaration of trust “respecting any land” to be manifested and proved by a signed written document by the person able to declare the trust (or authorised agent). No such clear, contemporaneous instrument is identified; bare assertion of a foreign arrangement cannot satisfy a domestic statutory writing requirement.

The mortgage-related documents are equally deficient. They are not trust instruments but finance documents, equivocal as to any disposition of JEV’s beneficial interest. They do not unambiguously set out the terms of an express trust, its subject matter and beneficiaries, made by JEV as settlor. At best, they record how the parties wished the property to be perceived for lending purposes. Section 53(1)(b) demands strict compliance; informal or collateral references to EPF’s “beneficial” status are insufficient.

Nor can these documents retrospectively “confirm” an earlier undocumented express trust, or be recharacterised as giving rise to a resulting/constructive trust so as to escape section 53(1)(b), when JEV’s own case is that there was an express arrangement.

Accordingly, Iris House was JEV’s asset at the time of transfer. The post-award disposition, with no adequate value and timed to defeat enforcement, falls squarely within section 423 and should be set aside in Steel Horizon’s favor.

Jade Energy Ventures’ disposal of Iris House is a transaction at an undervalue within section 423.

First, Jade Energy Ventures was the registered legal owner. Section 423 is engaged if an asset of the debtor is removed from its estate for the purpose of prejudicing creditors. The transfer occurred *after* Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce its award—a classic “eve of enforcement” disposition, strongly evidencing a section 423 purpose.

To avoid section 423, Jade Energy Ventures must show there was no depletion because Iris House was already held on trust for Emerald Pension Fund. That contention fails on both fact and law.

On the facts, Jade Energy Ventures relies on (i) an alleged prior beneficial ownership under “foreign law” and (ii) two mortgage-related documents. There is no indication of clear, cogent evidence explaining the foreign-law arrangement or demonstrating that beneficial title ever left Jade Energy Ventures. The mortgage documents on their face are financing instruments, not unequivocal trust declarations.

On the law, section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 requires that a declaration of trust of land be “manifested and proved” by some writing “signed by some person who is able to declare such trust.” Compliance is strict. It is critical *who* signs and in *what capacity*. If the signatories acted as agents for Jade Energy Ventures in mortgage transactions, that does not, without explicit authority to declare trusts, satisfy section 53(1)(b). A trust cannot be retrofitted out of routine security paperwork.

Absent a valid, properly evidenced trust, Iris House was a Jade Energy Ventures asset at the time of transfer. The transfer, shortly after enforcement permission was granted, plainly put valuable property beyond Steel Horizon’s reach, for no commensurate consideration, and thus constitutes a transaction at an undervalue under section 423.

Iris House was an asset of Jade Energy Ventures (“JEV”) when Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce the arbitral award. The subsequent transfer to Emerald Pension Fund (“EPF”) is therefore a classic transaction at an undervalue designed to defeat creditors within section 423 of the Insolvency Act 1986.

First, any alleged pre‑existing beneficial interest of EPF must comply with section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925: “a declaration of trust respecting any land… must be manifested and proved by some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust.” For English land, foreign‑law arrangements cannot sidestep mandatory English formalities. JEV has not produced a contemporaneous, properly executed declaration identifying trust property, beneficiaries, and terms, signed by JEV in its capacity as beneficial owner.

The two mortgage‑related documents are, at most, collateral statements to a lender, not instruments deliberately effecting or evidencing a trust. They do not clearly constitute, or “manifest and prove,” a present declaration of trust over Iris House. Most critically, they are not shown to have been signed by JEV qua beneficial owner declaring itself trustee for EPF; they appear in the context of security documentation, signed by agents whose authority to declare trusts is neither pleaded nor proved. Section 53(1)(b) is a strict statutory gateway; informal or incidental references in finance documents cannot retrospectively validate an otherwise non‑compliant trust.

Absent a valid prior trust, JEV remained the beneficial owner of Iris House until the impugned transfer. That transfer occurred only after Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce, strongly evidencing a section 423 purpose: putting a valuable asset beyond the reach of a major creditor. Since beneficial ownership passed out of JEV for no proper commercial consideration and with a purpose to prejudice Steel Horizon, section 423 is squarely engaged and the disposition should be set aside.

Section 423 is engaged if (1) Jade Energy Ventures (“JEV”) entered a transaction at an undervalue, and (2) one purpose was to put assets beyond creditors’ reach. Both conditions are met.

First, JEV was the registered legal owner of Iris House. The purported “pre‑existing” beneficial ownership of Emerald Pension Fund (“EPF”) rests entirely on two mortgage-related documents. Those documents are not framed as trust instruments, were executed in a financing context, and at most are equivocal as to beneficial entitlement. They cannot retroactively erase JEV’s beneficial ownership without satisfying section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925.

Section 53(1)(b) requires “a declaration of trust… manifested and proved by some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust.” The alleged trust is said to have been declared by JEV as landowner. Yet the signatures relied upon are those of representatives signing mortgage documents in that capacity, not as explicit settlors of EPF’s beneficial interest. There is no clear, unequivocal written declaration by JEV, qua beneficial owner, that it held Iris House on trust for EPF. Ambiguous, incidental wording in security documentation is insufficient to “manifest and prove” the alleged trust.

The fallback reliance on an arrangement under foreign law is likewise deficient: no cogent evidence of its content, validity, or compliance with English formality rules as to land is provided. English law still insists on section 53(1)(b) compliance for trusts of land.

Accordingly, Iris House was JEV’s beneficial asset until its transfer to EPF, shortly after Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce its award. That transfer was for no, or grossly inadequate, consideration and timed plainly to defeat enforcement. It is therefore a transaction at an undervalue within section 423, and the court should grant relief restoring Iris House (or its value) for Steel Horizon’s benefit.

Jade Energy Ventures should prevail because Iris House was never part of its beneficial estate and therefore could not be the subject of a “transaction at an undervalue” under section 423.

First, section 423 requires a disposition by the debtor of its own beneficial property, causing a depletion of the debtor’s assets. On the facts, Emerald Pension Fund was always the genuine beneficial owner. Jade Energy Ventures held, at most, the legal title as a bare trustee—initially under a valid foreign-law arrangement, and then, if necessary, under an English-law trust.

Second, section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925 is satisfied. That provision requires “signed writing” evidencing a declaration of trust of land; it does not mandate a formal trust instrument nor particular wording. The mortgage-related documents were signed by duly authorised representatives of Jade Energy Ventures—the legal owner—and explicitly treated Emerald Pension Fund as the beneficial owner. That is classic “signed writing” by the landowner manifesting the trust. A company can only act through such signatories; to say that an act by its officers is not an act by the “landowner” misunderstands corporate personality.

Third, section 53(1)(b) is an evidential requirement, not a weapon to defeat a genuinely intended trust in favour of a pension fund. The mortgage documents are objective, contemporaneous, and commercially coherent evidence that Jade Energy Ventures did not own Iris House beneficially. At most, the later transfer simply perfected Emerald Pension Fund’s existing equitable rights and left Jade Energy Ventures’ net asset position unchanged.

Because Jade Energy Ventures never had a beneficial interest to dispose of, there was no “transaction at an undervalue” and no relevant prejudice to Steel Horizon. The section 423 claim must therefore fail.

Section 423 IA 1986 is only engaged if there is a “transaction at an undervalue” involving Jade Energy Ventures’ own beneficial asset. If Iris House was at all material times held by Jade on trust for Emerald Pension Fund, then Jade’s transfer was merely the divestment of bare legal title and did not deplete its estate. On that footing, there is no “transaction at an undervalue” and no relevant “victim”.

The contemporaneous mortgage documentation is critical. It identifies Emerald as the beneficial owner and was executed by those with authority to bind Jade, the registered proprietor. That satisfies section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925, which requires only “some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust”; it does not insist on any particular form, nor does it prohibit the use of agents. Execution by Jade’s authorised signatories is in law execution by Jade itself, so Steel Horizon’s attempt to distinguish “the landowner” from “an agent” is artificial.

Moreover, the documents are confirmatory of an existing beneficial entitlement rooted in the prior foreign-law arrangement. Section 53(1)(b) regulates the *declaration* of new equitable interests in land, not the recognition in writing of trusts already arising from earlier arrangements or from resulting/constructive trust principles; such trusts are expressly outside its scope (s.53(2)). At minimum, the written confirmations are powerful evidence of a pre‑existing trust and Emerald’s equitable ownership.

Accordingly, at the time Steel Horizon acquired its award and sought to enforce, Jade’s beneficial interest in Iris House was nil. The later transfer could not have been “for a consideration the value of which… is significantly less” than the value provided by Jade, because Jade provided only bare legal title. With no diminution of Jade’s real assets and no undervalue transaction, section 423 is not engaged and Steel Horizon’s claim must fail.

Jade Energy Ventures should prevail because Iris House was never an asset beneficially available to Jade’s creditors, so there was no “transaction at an undervalue” under section 423 Insolvency Act 1986.

First, on the facts, Emerald Pension Fund was always the true beneficial owner. The property was acquired and held in the context of a pension arrangement; Jade’s role was that of legal title-holder for the Fund. Section 423 applies only to dispositions of the debtor’s own property at an undervalue. Where a company holds only bare legal title on trust, transferring that legal title to the beneficiary does not deplete the company’s estate.

Second, the requirements of section 53(1)(b) Law of Property Act 1925 are satisfied. That provision only demands that a declaration of trust of land be “manifested and proved by some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust or by his will.” The two mortgage-related documents:

- expressly identify Emerald Pension Fund as the beneficial owner of Iris House;  
- are in writing; and  
- are signed by duly authorised representatives of Jade Energy Ventures, the very person “able to declare such trust.”

Section 53(1)(b) does not require the landowner’s *own hand* on the document; a company necessarily acts through officers and agents, and their signatures are sufficient manifestation of Jade’s intention.

Third, the registration and filing of those mortgage documents with Iris House treated as an asset of Emerald Pension Fund is powerful, objective confirmation of the trust and fully consistent with commercial reality. To let Steel Horizon invoke section 53(1)(b) to disregard a documented pension trust and seize pension assets would convert a formalities provision into an instrument of fraud, contrary to long‑standing equitable principle.

Because Jade never beneficially owned Iris House, there was no relevant “transaction at an undervalue,” and the section 423 claim must fail.

Section 423 IA 1986 is only engaged where there is a “transaction” by which the debtor’s own asset base is depleted at an undervalue. If Iris House was never beneficially owned by Jade Energy Ventures (JEV), or ceased to be so long before enforcement was sought, there was no relevant depletion and no transaction at an undervalue.

First, the evidence shows that Emerald Pension Fund was the true beneficial owner. The two mortgage-related documents, signed on behalf of JEV as the registered proprietor, expressly recorded Emerald as the beneficial owner. That is powerful contemporaneous evidence of the parties’ shared understanding and of an existing trust. Section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 requires only that a declaration of trust “be manifested and proved by some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust or by his will.” It does not require a freestanding, formal “trust deed,” nor does it require that the landowner sign otherwise than via duly authorised representatives.

Those mortgage documents satisfy the statute: they are written instruments, signed on behalf of the legal owner, and unequivocally recognising Emerald’s beneficial entitlement. They at least “manifest and prove” a subsisting trust; s.53(1)(b) is evidential, not constitutive. To insist on some additional, rigid formalism goes beyond the statutory language and mischaracterises its purpose.

Moreover, to the extent the beneficial interest arose under an earlier foreign-law arrangement or by way of resulting/constructive trust (e.g. Emerald providing value), s.53(2) exempts such trusts from the writing requirement altogether.

Accordingly, at the time of the impugned transfer, JEV held only bare legal title. The conveyance simply aligned legal with equitable ownership; no value was removed from JEV’s estate. Without a disposition of JEV’s own beneficial asset, section 423 cannot be engaged, and Steel Horizon’s claim must fail.

Section 423 is engaged only if Jade Energy Ventures (“Jade”) disposed of *its* own asset at an undervalue. If, as Jade contends, Iris House was at all material times held on trust for Emerald Pension Fund (“Emerald”), there was no depletion of Jade’s estate and nothing upon which section 423 can operate.

First, the contemporaneous mortgage documentation is powerful, objective evidence that Emerald, not Jade, was the true beneficial owner. Those documents—signed by duly authorised representatives of Jade as registered proprietor—expressly record Emerald’s beneficial ownership. That satisfies section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925: a declaration of trust of land need only be “manifested and proved” in signed writing; it need not be created *by* that document, nor be in any particular form. The company’s officers signed as the landowner; the suggestion that they were somehow “mere agents” for this purpose seeks to re‑characterise standard corporate execution formalities into a technical nullity.

Second, to the extent Emerald’s beneficial interest first arose under the earlier foreign-law arrangement, English law will recognise that interest either as an express trust later evidenced in writing, or as a resulting/constructive trust falling outside section 53(1)(b) altogether (section 53(2)). In either case, Jade never enjoyed more than bare legal title.

Third, the later transfer of Iris House to Emerald Pension Fund simply aligned legal title with the pre‑existing beneficial interest. A trustee’s transfer of trust property to its beneficiary is not a transaction at an undervalue of the trustee’s own assets; it is performance of an existing obligation. Steel Horizon cannot claim prejudice in respect of property that was never available to Jade’s general creditors.

Accordingly, section 423 is not engaged and Steel Horizon’s claim must fail.

ShelterCo should prevail because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) cannot, as a matter of statutory construction and principle, retrospectively unsettle vested service‑charge rights in respect of pre‑commencement costs.

First, the leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 together conferred a clear, existing entitlement on ShelterCo to recover (i) costs of repairing and making the building safe, and (ii) reasonable management and legal costs incurred in administering and enforcing the service‑charge regime. Those rights crystallised when the relevant liabilities were incurred. There is a strong presumption against retrospective interference with accrued contractual and property rights absent express wording. The BSA contains no clear language invalidating recovery of costs incurred before its commencement.

Second, Parliament built temporal limits into the BSA’s leaseholder‑protection scheme. The natural reading is that restrictions apply to “relevant measures” and “relevant defects” addressed after the operative dates. Where the landlord’s liability to third‑party contractors has already arisen, the BSA should not be read to strip the landlord of its parallel recovery route under existing leases. To do so would convert the Act into a retroactive reallocation of historic liabilities, contrary to basic rule‑of‑law standards.

Third, the remedial and interim fire‑safety measures were necessary to comply with statutory and regulatory duties following expert inspections. Leaseholders always bore, via service charge, the risk that compliance with evolving safety standards would generate substantial expenditure. The BSA was designed to regulate and constrain that allocation prospectively, not to render historic, contractually recoverable outlays irrecoverable.

Finally, legal and professional costs incurred to establish and administer service‑charge recovery are classic management expenses, long accepted as recoverable where the lease permits, provided they are reasonably incurred. There is nothing in the BSA that displaces that orthodoxy for liabilities predating its commencement.

Accordingly, ShelterCo remains entitled to recover the pre‑commencement fire‑safety and remedial costs, including associated legal expenses, through the service charge.

ShelterCo should prevail because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) cannot retrospectively extinguish vested contractual and statutory rights to recover costs validly incurred before the relevant commencement dates.

First, the leases clearly entitle ShelterCo to recover costs of “necessary compliance and repair” by service charge. Under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, such charges are payable insofar as they are reasonably incurred and of reasonable standard. The fire safety works and precautionary measures were plainly necessary to comply with statutory obligations and to protect life and property. Absent express legislative wording to the contrary, Parliament is presumed not to interfere retrospectively with existing contractual bargains.

Second, the BSA 2022 contains a carefully staged commencement scheme and detailed transitional provisions. Where Parliament intended to cap or bar recovery of certain “relevant measures”, it did so prospectively. The tenants’ construction, which would retroactively invalidate or limit recovery of costs already incurred or irreversibly committed before commencement, would create uncertainty, upset settled expectations, and amount to a windfall for leaseholders at the landlord’s expense—contrary to the principle against expropriation without clear words.

Third, legal and professional costs incurred to put in place the mechanism for recovery are themselves part and parcel of the remedial project and fall within the leases’ broad wording on compliance and management costs. The Act does not distinguish between physical and associated legal costs nor purport to rewrite existing cost-recovery clauses for past expenditure.

Finally, limiting ShelterCo’s recovery here would seriously undermine the policy of the BSA itself: ensuring that necessary fire-safety remediation is carried out. If freeholders cannot rely on historic service charge rights for pre‑commencement obligations, they may be deterred from acting promptly in future high‑risk situations.

Accordingly, the court should hold that the BSA 2022 does not bar recovery of pre‑commencement costs and confirm ShelterCo’s right to recover them via service charges.

ShelterCo should succeed because Parliament has not clearly displaced its vested contractual and statutory rights to recover these particular costs.

First, there is a strong presumption against retrospective interference with private law rights. The leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 together conferred a pre‑existing entitlement to recover “costs of repair, maintenance and compliance with statutory requirements” through service charges. The fire‑safety defects and the bulk of the remedial scheme were identified, commissioned, and contractually committed to before the relevant provisions of the Building Safety Act 2022 came into force. Absent clear wording, the Act cannot be read to unwind or re‑allocate historic liabilities that had already attached to the property and its leaseholders.

Second, the Building Safety Act’s leaseholder‑protection regime is tightly drafted and time‑bound. Where Parliament wished to cap, extinguish, or re‑characterise service charge liability for “relevant defects,” it did so expressly and with detailed transitional machinery. Nothing in those provisions states that costs already incurred, or contractual and professional fees necessarily incurred in order to operate an existing service charge mechanism, are irrecoverable. At most, the Act regulates future demands for protected categories of remediation; it does not nullify the underlying right to recover sunk costs properly incurred under the pre‑existing regime.

Third, any broader reading would create serious incompatibility with A1P1 ECHR and basic rule‑of‑law principles by expropriating the landlord’s only realistic economic mechanism (service charges) for costs it was legally obliged to incur to keep the building safe. A proportionate construction is available: the Act limits future recovery of specified post‑commencement costs, but leaves intact ShelterCo’s entitlement to recoup pre‑commencement remediation and associated legal costs where they were reasonably incurred under the leases and section 19 of the 1985 Act.

ShelterCo should prevail because the Building Safety Act 2022 cannot fairly or lawfully be construed to strip away vested contractual and statutory rights in respect of pre‑commencement costs.

First, the leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 together gave ShelterCo a clear, pre‑existing entitlement to recover necessary repair, compliance, and associated professional and legal costs through the service charge, subject to reasonableness. Those rights were part of the commercial bargain struck with each leaseholder and underpin the economic viability of owning and managing the block, particularly where ground rent income is minimal.

Second, there is a strong presumption against legislation operating retrospectively to disturb accrued rights or re‑characterise past events, absent clear words. Nothing in the Building Safety Act 2022 expressly invalidates historic service charge liabilities that had already arisen under existing leases. Any ambiguity in temporal scope must be resolved in favour of preserving contractual expectations and avoiding windfalls to leaseholders at the landlord’s expense.

Third, even if some elements of the Act apply to ongoing or future demands, the “costs in question” here include work specified, instructed, or incurred before the relevant provisions came into force, and the legal and professional steps then taken were integral to enforcing those pre‑existing rights. Those expenses crystallised before the Act’s commencement and therefore fall outside its new restrictions.

Finally, interpreting the Act to preclude recovery of historic costs would undermine the very objective of improving building safety: landlords would be disincentivised or unable to fund urgent remediation where leaseholders had expressly agreed to bear such costs. The proper construction is that the Act regulates future liabilities but does not retrospectively rewrite the financial incidents of these long leases. ShelterCo is therefore entitled to recover the disputed pre‑commencement costs via the service charge.

ShelterCo is entitled to recover the disputed costs via service charges because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) does not clearly and retrospectively abrogate existing contractual and statutory rights in respect of pre‑commencement expenditure.

First, the leases expressly permit recovery of necessary repair and compliance costs by service charge. Those rights are reinforced, not displaced, by the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985: so long as costs are reasonably incurred and works are of a reasonable standard, they are recoverable. Here, the remedial and precautionary fire‑safety measures were mandated by inspection findings and regulatory expectations for a building over 18m; they are paradigmatic examples of “necessary” works.

Second, Parliament is presumed not to interfere retrospectively with vested rights absent clear language. The BSA’s cost‑protection regime is framed prospectively: its limitations apply to specified “relevant measures” and “relevant defects” and regulate what can be demanded after commencement, not the legal character of liabilities already accrued under pre‑existing leases. Nothing in the Act plainly extinguishes landlords’ rights to recover costs already incurred, nor legal and professional fees reasonably incurred to make those recoveries effective.

Third, many of the challenged sums are for interim safety measures and preparatory professional advice predating commencement of the relevant BSA provisions. To treat them as barred would create arbitrary cut‑offs unrelated to legislative text, undermining legal certainty and the careful balancing of interests in the BSA.

Accordingly, the court should hold that the BSA 2022 does not retrospectively bar ShelterCo from relying on its pre‑existing lease and 1985 Act entitlements to recover the pre‑commencement fire‑safety and remedial costs through the service charge.

ShelterCo cannot recover these costs through the service charge because the Building Safety Act 2022 (BSA) was expressly designed to break from the historic position under the leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, and to curb landlords’ ability to pass historic fire-safety failures onto leaseholders.

First, the BSA’s leaseholder protections (particularly the “relevant defect” and “relevant building” regime and the caps/ exclusions on remediation and interim-cost recovery) apply by reference to when costs are *demanded* or *sought* from leaseholders, not when the defect arose or when the landlord first incurred expenditure. Parliament’s clear objective was to deal with precisely these historic, pre-commencement fire‑safety defects in existing tall buildings like Lowbridge Towers (over 18m, predominantly residential). To treat “pre‑commencement” costs as wholly outside the regime would defeat that purpose and render the protections largely illusory.

Secondly, where ShelterCo (or an associated developer/landlord) bears responsibility for the defective external wall system, the BSA prohibits or strictly limits recovery of remediation and interim fire‑safety measures from qualifying leaseholders, regardless of lease wording. The Act is overtly interventionist and overrides inconsistent contractual service‑charge clauses.

Thirdly, legal and administrative costs incurred by ShelterCo to position itself to bill leaseholders are not “costs of remedying relevant defects” reasonably incurred for the building’s safety; they are costs of litigation and cost‑shifting strategy. Under both the BSA protections and s.19 and s.20C of the 1985 Act, such costs are not reasonably recoverable via the service charge and, in any event, should be disallowed as contrary to the new protective regime.

Accordingly, the court should construe the BSA purposively so that pre‑commencement fire‑safety and related legal costs cannot be recovered from the Occupants through service charges.

The Occupants should prevail because, properly construed, the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) restricts ShelterCo from passing these fire‑safety costs through service charges, including where works or liabilities originated before commencement.

First, Lowbridge Towers is more than 18m high and plainly a “relevant building”. The BSA’s core purpose is to protect leaseholders from historic building safety defects and to prevent freeholders from using service‑charge machinery to shift the cost of their own failures. The court must therefore adopt a purposive reading rather than allowing pre‑existing lease wording to defeat a flagship consumer‑protection statute.

Second, the BSA limitations bite when costs become “recoverable” or “payable” as service charges. Even if some works or liabilities arose pre‑commencement, they are not recoverable until validly demanded through the service charge mechanism—i.e. post‑commencement—and thus fall within the Act’s restrictions. ShelterCo’s characterisation of them as “historical” cannot override Parliament’s chosen trigger: recovery from leaseholders.

Third, to the extent any ambiguity exists about temporal scope, it must be resolved in favour of the protected class (leaseholders), consistent with established principles of interpreting remedial legislation and, as to the leases, contra proferentem.

Fourth, legal and management costs incurred in order to position ShelterCo to bill leaseholders for remediation are not “costs of repair or compliance” reasonably incurred for the building under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985. They are landlord‑side tactical expenditure aimed at avoiding the very protections the BSA introduces, and are therefore irrecoverable.

Finally, allowing ShelterCo to rely on historic lease clauses and the 1985 Act to circumvent the BSA would render the new protections hollow for precisely the group—occupants of high‑risk existing buildings—that Parliament intended to prioritise. The court should hold that the BSA bars recovery of these costs through service charges.

ShelterCo is barred – in whole or substantial part – from recovery.

Lowbridge Towers is a “relevant building” over 11m/5 storeys; the cladding and external fire-safety problems are paradigm “relevant defects.” Schedule 8 of the Building Safety Act 2022 was enacted precisely to prevent leaseholders from bearing historic life‑critical safety costs which they neither caused nor controlled. Any construction of the statute that permits wholesale recoupment of pre‑commencement remediation costs would undermine that core protective purpose.

Schedule 8 is drafted to bite on *service charge liabilities*, not merely on the timing of physical works. The relevant trigger is the demand or recovery of sums from leaseholders after commencement, not the date the landlord happened to incur or commit to the expenditure. Where Parliament intended purely prospective effect, it said so expressly elsewhere in the Act; in contrast, Sch 8 is framed to limit what “may be passed on” in the future, including in respect of past defects and historic spending.

ShelterCo’s reliance on lease terms and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 cannot override those later statutory limits. Section 27A of the 1985 Act and Sch 8 operate together: only sums both contractually due *and* statutorily permitted are recoverable. To the extent lease clauses purport to shift prohibited remediation or associated legal costs, they are rendered ineffective by Sch 8 and, in any event, would fall foul of the reasonableness test and consumer‑protection principles.
